description: We're a team working on Dancing with the SARs, using NASA-ISRO's new NISAR radar satellite to detect and map real-world surface changes like floods and wildfires, even through clouds and at night.
summary: Dancing with the SARs is an interactive web app by team SkySense that uses NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar to show how Earth’s surface changed in Sri Lanka and beyond, from June to November 2026, through wet and dry spells. It has seven stories: Matara, Minneriya, Senanayake Samudraya, and Colombo Port in Sri Lanka, floods in Thailand and Assam, and the Devighat disaster in Nepal. Each story offers a before/after view, a time-lapse, a rain time series, and Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 context, with tabs for what we see, data used, limits, and likely physical drivers, so each change is read alongside independent data. Radar’s HH and HV channels and their ratio are shown as red, green, and blue, so colors mean the same everywhere. A rain test at Nawalapitiya, Ratnapura, and Ampara checks whether the radar signal follows rainfall and soil moisture, using NASA GPM IMERG rain, AMSR2 soil moisture, and forest controls, and corrects the step between provisional and validated NISAR products. We state limits openly: provisional data, coarse rainfall, and some sites without field confirmation. The app makes radar data readable for officials, farmers, and students and suggests future uses such as flood mapping through cloud and reservoir monitoring.
details:
SKYSENSE: DANCING WITH THE SARs

Team SkySense: Anuththara Divyanjalie, Muditha Kumara, Mayumi Maleesha

Project Folder: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1TNQuHOK1a2CKP27EgGI2LnRJDvmnfZTM?usp=sharing

Code and processing scripts: https://github.com/anuththara325/dancing-with-the-sars_SkySense

WHAT IT IS?

SkySense is an interactive web app that turns radar data from the NASA-ISRO NISAR satellite into plain-language stories of how Earth's surface changed between June and November 2026. In the rainy season, optical satellites mostly see clouds. Radar sees the ground, day or night. We chose seven places in four countries (Thailand, India, Nepal, and Sri Lanka), and we also ran a "rain test" at three more places in Sri Lanka to check whether the radar colors really follow rain and soil wetness.

1. WHAT DOES IT DO AND HOW DOES IT WORK?

SkySense is an interactive web app that turns NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar into seven short stories of surface change, from June to November 2026. Radar makes its own signal, so it sees the ground through cloud, day or night. Each story page shows the images first, then short tabs: Key takeaway, What we see, Data used, Limits, Why it may happen, and Where is this (with a Google Maps link).

Every story has:

  • a before/after slider and a time-lapse,
  • three views of the same place: NISAR (L-band radar), Sentinel-1 (C-band radar) and Sentinel-2 (optical),
  • a clickable time series with rainfall,
  • a change layer showing which radar channel picked up the change.

The seven places:

  • Thailand (flood): open water in the study box rose from under 1% to about 17% in NISAR after the wettest spell of the season, and was still about 14% on 12 October. Sentinel-1 shows the same timing.
  • Assam, India (flood): about 45 km² turned darker after heavy July rain, then brighter in the dry season, in both NISAR and Sentinel-1.
  • Devighat, Nepal (surge and landslide): a lasting change corridor along the Trishuli river, about 3–6% of the box, after the 26 August 2026 event.
  • Matara, Sri Lanka (rain): about 2.3 km² of land newly dark on 18 October, after the wettest three days of the season. This is water-like land, not confirmed flooding.
  • Minneriya, Sri Lanka (tanks and farming, preliminary): the dark area in the irrigated field zone falls through the season.
  • Senanayake Samudraya, Sri Lanka (reservoir): less open water by September than in the June outline, in both radar and optical, with Irrigation Department storage as a direction-only check.
  • Colombo Port, Sri Lanka (human activity): terminal pixels change between almost every pair of passes (about 28–44%), while a nearby city block stays near 1%.

Learning tools

New to radar? A plain-words guide covering what radar is, why it works through cloud, what bands and polarizations mean, and how to read a story. Its “Same place, two views” section lets visitors flip between radar and an optical picture.

Which polarizations show the change?

  • HH (shown red): sent and received horizontally. Smooth water and wet ground look dark, while double bounce off structures or flooded plants looks bright.
  • HV (shown green): sent horizontally, received vertically. It comes from scattering among leaves, stems and rough ground, so it follows vegetation and ground cover.
  • Across the seven sites, HH showed water-type darkening over a larger area, while HV followed vegetation.
  • A Radar Vegetation Index panel (RVI = 4 × HV / (HH + HV)) for three places shows relative plant-like scattering, never biomass.

Rain test: can NISAR feel the rain?

  • We asked whether the radar colour follows real rain and wet ground. At Nawalapitiya (hills), Ampara (dry zone) and Ratnapura (wet zone) we built time-lapses from morning and evening passes and compared them with rain in the previous 7 days (NASA GPM IMERG) and AMSR2 satellite soil moisture (how wet the top few centimetres of ground are).
  • HV (green) tracks the vegetation layer and the water it holds. Against 7-day rain: Nawalapitiya r = 0.73 morning, 0.60 evening (open land responded about twice as strongly as forest); Ampara r = 0.61 and 0.63 (weaker, and the page says so); Ratnapura r = 0.78 and 0.74.
  • HH (red) tracks the wetness of the ground. Against soil moisture: Ampara evening r = 0.75, Ratnapura evening r = 0.71. Over fixed bare and fallow pixels at Ampara, HH rose about 1.8 dB from the driest to the wettest date.
  • What is r? The correlation coefficient, from −1 to +1: near +1 means two things rise and fall together, near 0 means no link. With only 7 to 12 passes per place, we read these as a clear direction, not an exact measurement.
  • Why we trust the direction: the same pattern appears in three very different places, on two passes a day, against two independent sources.
  • Limits: one season, provisional data, coarse rain and soil data, no field probes. This is a test of the idea, not a soil-moisture service.

Colours

Red = HH, Green = HV, Blue = HH minus HV (dB), following the NASA SVS 5661 recipe. Sentinel-1 uses the same logic with VV and VH. Never compare dB for dB between sensors.

What do you get from this?

Possible uses (not existing services) for scientists, resource managers, teachers, decision-makers and the public: showing where and when the surface changed, how water moves through the season, and how rain relates to the radar signal.

2. WHAT BENEFITS DOES IT HAVE?

  • It makes radar understandable. Most people have never seen a radar image. The guide, the colour recipe and the before/after sliders let a non-expert see what changed and where.
  • It works when optical satellites cannot see: cloud, heavy rain, night.
  • It is honest. Every page lists its limits, uses the words "consistent with" instead of "proves", and shows what radar cannot tell (for example, dark radar means a smooth surface, not always flood water).
  • It links radar to rain and soil moisture, so users can see timing, not only pictures.
  • It uses free, open data and open code, so anyone can repeat or extend it.
  • It is simple to open: a web link, or a zip that opens by double-clicking index.html.

3. WHAT IS THE INTENDED IMPACT?

  • Public and teachers: a clear first step into radar remote sensing, with plain words and Sri Lankan examples.
  • Resource and disaster managers (for example irrigation, disaster management, agriculture): a quick look at when and where the surface changed, how it lines up with rain, and how far the signal can be trusted.
  • Scientists and students: a checked, caveated set of NISAR examples with dates, methods, validation steps and the claims we withdrew.
  • Local impact: four of the seven stories and the whole Rain test are in Sri Lanka. These are places where floods, reservoir levels and farming decide people's lives.
  • Future: a template for adding a new place (clip, process, add rain, add to the app) as validated NISAR data arrives.

4. TOOLS, LANGUAGES, HARDWARE AND SOFTWARE

Data

  • NISAR L2 GCOV (NASA-ISRO), provisional release from 17 June 2026 and validated release from 21 October 2026, from ASF DAAC. Bands HH and HV, L-band.
  • Sentinel-1 (OPERA RTC-S1 via ASF) and Sentinel-2 L2A (AWS Earth Search) from Copernicus.
  • NASA GPM IMERG daily rainfall (GES DISC Giovanni), NASA POWER (MERRA-2) rainfall, AMSR2 LPRM soil moisture (GES DISC).
  • ESA WorldCover 2021 (forest mask).
  • NASA SVS 5661 colour recipe. Context sources include NASA Earth Observatory, news agencies and Irrigation Department figures (compiled by Macro Lab).

Languages and software

  • Python for processing: GDAL, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow and Matplotlib. Scripts clip each scene, apply smoothing and masks, measure change, compare with rain and soil moisture, and export the images.
  • HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript for the web app (no heavy framework). Images are optimised as WebP.
  • Playwright for automatic page tests (13 pages checked for broken images and errors).
  • GitHub and GitHub Pages for hosting.
  • Claude (Anthropic) helped us write and check scripts, the web app and the draft text.

Hardware

  • Ordinary laptops (a Mac, and a Windows laptop running Ubuntu through WSL). Large NISAR files were downloaded from ASF DAAC with an Earthdata login, so no special hardware was needed.

5. HOW IS IT CREATIVE?

  • One page, three satellites, same place: the story pages put NISAR, Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 side by side so people can see what radar sees that a camera misses.
  • A channel switch that lets users view composite, HH only or HV only. It shows polarization instead of describing it.
  • Rain-linked time series and time-lapses that show a signal and the rain behind it on the same page.
  • "Same place, two views": a toggle between radar and an optical picture, so a beginner learns by comparing.
  • A role picker ("What do you get from this?") that shows what each kind of user could use this for.
  • We tested our own ideas and kept only what held up. A per-pixel "stays wet longer" map looked convincing but failed a reproducibility test, so we removed it instead of presenting it.
  • A modern, simple design: our SkySense logo, red and green for HH and HV, and short readable pages.

6. WHAT FACTORS DID WE CONSIDER?

  • Trust over drama. We used "consistent with" throughout, never compared NISAR and Sentinel-1 dB for dB (different wavelengths), and never mixed provisional and validated products without a measured correction.
  • Data quality. Speckle, swath edges, scene flags and an instrument gap (27 July to 10 August) were handled or avoided.
  • Audience. Beginners, teachers, managers and scientists need different things. We added a guide, a role picker and limits on every page.
  • Local relevance. Sri Lanka's rainy seasons, reservoirs, ports and paddy lands.
  • Accessibility of access. One link, no login, no install.
  • Responsible AI use. We disclose that Claude assisted us and we check data and conclusions ourselves.
  • Credits and rights. NASA, ESA/Copernicus and every data source are credited; we do not use or alter NASA logos.

7. HOW WE FOUND OUR PLACES

Choosing places was one of the hardest and slowest parts of the project.

  • NISAR provisional data only start on 17 June 2026, repeat every 12 days, and have a gap from 27 July to 10 August. So for any place we get only about 10 to 20 dates, and an event can fall between two passes.
  • Within that window, Sri Lanka had few large, clearly dated events that radar could show cleanly. We searched many Sri Lankan and nearby scenarios (for example Colombo Port, Matara, Minneriya, Senanayake Samudraya, Kotmale reservoir, Lower Malwathu Oya land clearing and more), downloaded the scenes and checked each one for a real, repeatable signal.
  • We kept the places where the signal was clear and checkable, and set aside the ones that were small or unclear (Kotmale and Malwathu Oya).
  • Because Sri Lanka alone did not give enough strong, dated events, we added well-known regional events in the same period (Thailand and Assam floods, the Nepal surge and landslide). They show what radar can do for large events, next to our Sri Lankan stories.
  • We checked every candidate for swath edges, scene flags and valid coverage, and withdrew several early results that turned out to be noise. The final list is shorter than the list we started with.
  • The result is seven stories, plus three Sri Lankan places for the Rain test.

8. WHY THREE VIEWS OF EACH PLACE

Each story puts NISAR (L-band radar), Sentinel-1 (C-band radar) and Sentinel-2 (optical) side by side on purpose.

  • It puts radar in the spotlight. In the rainy season the optical picture is often cloudy, hazy or too late, while radar still shows the ground. Seeing the two next to each other makes that point without a long explanation.
  • Sentinel-1 is a second radar. When two radars agree on timing, we trust the signal more. It also fills the gaps in NISAR's 12-day cycle.
  • Different wavelengths see different things: L-band goes deeper into vegetation, C-band responds more to the surface. So we compare timing and direction, never dB for dB.
  • Optical is used only as a picture, to give people something familiar to compare against.

9. WHAT MORE DID WE DO

  • Two sensors for cross-checks. Sentinel-1 was added to fill NISAR's gaps (Thailand, Assam).
  • HH vs HV comparison across all seven sites.
  • A Rain test at three places with morning and evening passes. This includes quad-pol evening passes at Ampara and Ratnapura, shown separately.
  • Provisional-to-validated correction. At Nawalapitiya we measured the offset between provisional and validated NISAR data on forest, which should not change, and corrected for it (about +0.35 dB HH and +0.11 dB HV on the morning pass).
  • Vegetation density (RVI) at three places. At Ampara, river-valley blocks rise from about 0.6 in early July to about 0.75 in late August and then ease, while forest stays flat at about 1.04 to 1.07. A split test on 4,332 blocks gave +1.45 dB HV-minus-HH on the even dates against +0.03 dB for the forest control, with 76% reproducing. This is consistent with crop growth in cultivated land. We do not claim crop type, planting or harvest dates.
  • A beginner guide, a role picker, a modern design, a logo, and tests on every page before launch.
  • Open code: processing scripts and the app are in our public GitHub repository.

10. LIMITATIONS WE FACED, AND HOW WE HANDLED THEM

  • Provisional data. All NISAR scenes before 21 October are provisional. We say so on every page, never mix products, and measured the offset to validated data at Nawalapitiya. Ampara and Ratnapura validated scenes are left out where the offset was not measured.
  • Few dates. NISAR repeats every 12 days, and there is a gap from 27 July to 10 August. Events are only bracketed between passes. We added Sentinel-1 to fill some gaps.
  • No ground truth. We had no gauges, field surveys or official flood extents of our own. We compare with rainfall, soil moisture, optical images, news and Irrigation Department data, and use "consistent with" instead of "proves".
  • Dark does not always mean flood water. Wet bare soil, ponded paddy and radar shadow also look dark, and flooded vegetation can be bright. We say so on the pages and use HH, HV and the ratio together.
  • Coarse rain. IMERG is about 10 km and POWER about 50 km. We use it for timing, not local amounts.
  • Early mistakes. Our first numbers were inflated by speckle, hand-drawn boxes and swath-edge fill. We rebuilt with smoothing, land masks and valid masks and withdrew the earlier claims. We also dropped a "drying time" map after our own test failed (see below).
  • Weaker result at Ampara. The Ampara rain relationship is weaker (r about 0.6) than at the other two places, and the page says so.
  • Cloud often blocks optical images in the rainy season. Optical is used as a picture only, never for numbers.
  • Sentinel-1 at 30 m cannot resolve small structures, so Port analysis relies on NISAR.
  • Event facts. Some event names and dates came from news and agency reports and are given as context, not as validation of our measured areas.
  • Time. This was a two-day hackathon; each place needed clipping, statistics, rain, optical context and web exports. 

11. WHAT WE TESTED AND DROPPED

We built a per-pixel map of where ground "stays wet longer" after rain. It looked coherent, but when we split the data into odd and even dates it did not reproduce (correlation near zero). We removed it from the app and made no claim from it. The box-level wetness signal (r = 0.73 on the morning pass and 0.60 on the evening pass) did hold up, and is what we present.

 

12. WHAT IS STILL REMAINING (FUTURE WORK)

  • Re-run every story on validated NISAR data and report any differences.
  • Real validation: compare with official flood extents, river and rain gauges, and field or drone photos, and publish the accuracy.
  • Better classification with HH, HV and the ratio together, using many date pairs and thresholds.
  • Time and temperature of drying: needs more passes, local rain gauges, and terrain and land-cover controls.
  • Automatic pipeline: pull new NISAR and Sentinel-1 scenes through the ASF API and update the app.
  • A web map where any visitor can pick their own town, plus population, land cover and terrain layers.
  • Other NISAR strengths: interferometry (centimetre-scale ground movement for landslides and subsidence), forest and biomass change, glaciers and sea ice.
  • More places and seasons, and working with Sri Lankan partners such as the Disaster Management Centre, the Irrigation Department and the Department of Agriculture.
  • Sinhala and Tamil versions and classroom activities.

13.FEASIBILITY ANALYSIS

 Technical feasibility: proven.

  • The whole chain already works end to end: download NISAR from ASF, clip and process with Python, add rain and optical context, export images, and publish a static web app.
  • It was built and tested in two days on ordinary laptops. The app runs from one link, or from one extracted folder, with no server, database or login.
  • Adding a new place follows the same steps each time (clip, process, add rain, add to the app).

Data feasibility: good, with limits.

  • NISAR data are free and open. The same products keep arriving, and validated data have been available since 21 October 2026.
  • Limits: all earlier scenes are provisional, the repeat is 12 days, and there was a gap from 27 July to 10 August. We handle this by labelling data, not mixing products, and adding Sentinel-1 to fill gaps.

Scientific feasibility: sound, with conclusions kept modest.

  • The methods are standard (backscatter change detection with smoothing, masks and control areas).
  • Results agree across sensors (NISAR and Sentinel-1) and across places. The rain relationship holds at three different places on both morning and evening passes.
  • We tested our own ideas and removed one that did not reproduce. What we claim is "consistent with", not proof. Confirming accuracy needs ground data (gauges, field surveys, official flood extents).

Operational feasibility: realistic for the intended users.

  • Users need only a web browser. A teacher, manager or journalist can open a story and read what radar saw and what it cannot say.
  • Running costs are very low: free data, free hosting on GitHub Pages and no servers.
  • The app is a learning and first-look tool. It is not an official warning or mapping service, and it says so.
  • Scalability: possible in stages.
  • Now: seven stories plus a three-place Rain test, processed by hand with our scripts.
  • Next: automate download and processing through the ASF programme interface, and add places and seasons.
  • Later: a map where visitors pick their own town, and finer rain and land-cover layers.
  • A true operational service would need validated NISAR data, automatic tasking and ground truth.

Main risks and how we handle them

  • Provisional data may change: we label it, do not mix products, and plan a re-run on validated data.
  • No ground truth: we use cautious wording and name the data we would need.
  • Coarse rainfall: we use it for timing only.
  • Free data servers can fail for a while: we keep processed images in the app, so it does not depend on live servers.
  • Time and team size: the scripts are repeatable, and the code is public so others can help.

Overall: technically and operationally feasible now as a learning and first-look tool; feasible as a monitoring service only with validated data, automation and local ground truth.

DATA, CREDITS AND AI DISCLOSURE

NISAR L2 GCOV (NASA-ISRO) via ASF DAAC. NASA SVS 5661 colour recipe. Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2026): Sentinel-1 (OPERA RTC-S1, ASF) and Sentinel-2 L2A (AWS Earth Search). Rain: NASA GPM IMERG and NASA POWER. Soil moisture: AMSR2 LPRM. Land cover: ESA WorldCover 2021. Thailand context: NASA Earth Observatory, 9 Oct 2026. Reservoir storage series compiled by Macro Lab from Irrigation Department data (not an official publication). No NASA logos are used or altered.

AI disclosure: the analysis scripts, the web app and the drafting of text were created with assistance from Claude (Anthropic).
